items.title: Ignite 2026: What's new in Microsoft Defender & Sentinel
items.summary: At Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re announcing new innovations across Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Sentinel that bring security operations and threat protection closer together, help organizations get ahead of attacks, secure AI agents and strengthen protection across critical workloads. The foundation for agentic security: Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender now includes the full breadth of SIEM capabilities and 90-days of built-in Defender data. Protection before the patch : Vulnerability shielding in Defender autonomously protects exposed systems before and during active attacks, giving security teams more time to deploy permanent patches to vulnerabilities. Protect AI agents wherever they run: Manage security posture for third-party agent platforms, prevent device code phishing and extend runtime protection for local AI agents on Windows. Protect people where they work: Extend defenses against browser-based attacks, malicious QR codes in Teams, and synthetic media threats. Together, these innovations build on a shared foundation of signals, actuators, and coordinated response to help security teams move faster and stop attacks before they spread. The foundation for agentic security ISOC now includes the full breadth of SIEM capabilities and 90 days of built-in retention The integrated SOC brings SIEM and threat protection together to provide the foundation for the agentic SOC. It gives people and agents shared context and the ability to see, understand, and act across the environment, so the security stack works as one system. Building on the September 23 announcement , core ISOC capabilities in Microsoft Defender are now generally available, including case management, playbooks, workbooks and UEBA. Workspace creation and third-party ingestion are also generally available. In addition, we are expanding the preview to include the full breadth of SIEM capabilities for eligible Defender customers, while enabling existing Sentinel customers to opt into ISOC. “What excites us most about ISOC is having a single pane of glass for security operations. Bringing SIEM and XDR together simplifies the analyst experience, while giving us an opportunity to optimize ingestion and automation costs.” - Farhan Nadeem, Senior Security Officer, Government of Nunavut New capabilities available in preview include 90 days of built-in Defender data retention, SOC optimization recommendations, Content Hub, detections as code, and automation audit logs. Figure 1. The Defender home dashboard showcasing the new Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) experience Simplify and scale security analytics with ingest-time data normalization Security data comes from diverse sources and formats, making analysis at scale complex. To simplify this, Microsoft is introducing ingest-time normalization, which standardizes data at time of ingestion, thereby simplifying queries, improving performance, and enabling reuse across detections, investigations, threat hunting, analytics, and agentic scenarios. This helps teams spend less time managing data, and more time stopping threats. It is now available in preview. Figure 2: Data normalization via parser management for query-ready security analytics. Protection before the patch AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery and exploitation. In October 2026 alone, 1,413 CVEs were disclosed, marking it the largest Patch Tuesday on record. Attackers can exploit vulnerabilities within hours, while organizations often need days or weeks to patch. That gap creates a critical window of exposure. Vulnerability shielding in Microsoft Defender, now in preview, helps close that gap by protecting vulnerable systems until patches are deployed. On by default in Microsoft Defender, vulnerability shielding applies targeted, temporary protection to vulnerable systems in the gap between exposure and remediation, buying defenders time before they can apply a permanent patch. This AI-based capability reasons over the latest threat intelligence and each organization’s unique environment to choose the narrowest effective protection. During an active attack, it applies controls autonomously, cutting off new attack paths for adversaries and limiting the impact to your organization. Learn more. Figure 3. Vulnerability shielding applied to a SQL server with a known public vulnerability Protect AI agents wherever they run AI agents now operate across cloud platforms and endpoints, accessing data, calling tools like MCP servers and APIs, and taking action, often with users’ own permissions. Security teams need visibility into what agents can access and the ability to stop them when compromised or manipulated. Assess posture for agents on third-party platforms Defender is extending security posture assessment to agents built on Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini, Google Vertex AI, and Anthropic Claude. Now in preview, they appear in the same AI agent inventory as your Microsoft Copilot Studio and Microsoft Foundry agents, with risk assessments and security recommendations, so you can prioritize risk across platforms. Bring them into scope by connecting their platforms to Agent 365 through connected platforms . Figure 4. Agent profile with security posture for Amazon Bedrock Agent Protect local agents at runtime Building on local AI agent discovery , runtime protection for local agents is now generally available* on Windows. Defender inspects critical points in the agent loop and can block malicious instructions before the agent acts. Supported agents include Claude Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, OpenClaw, ChatGPT Desktop (Chat) with the full list here . Each detection raises an alert with agent and session context, correlated into cases for your SOC; in Block mode, Defender also stops the action and notifies the user. Protect AI agents from attacks on trusted identities AI agent security goes beyond prompt injection. Attackers can exploit trusted identities and delegated permissions to manipulate agents without compromising them directly. New Microsoft Defender detections identify identity-based attacks, such as device-code phishing that compromises a developer’s GitHub account and enables misuse of GitHub Copilot CLI. Defender can detect suspicious activity and automatically disrupt attacks by disabling compromised Github accounts, revoking sessions, and triggering additional identity protections. Learn more about this emerging attack pattern in our latest threat research blog . Figure 5: Microsoft Defender detects a device code flow phishing attempt targeting a user’s GitHub account and disrupts the threat. Protect people where they work Attackers continue to target the places where people work and communicate. New protections across the browser, endpoint, email, and Microsoft Teams meetings help security teams identify malicious activity earlier and investigate it alongside signals from across the environment. Block browser lures and improve visibility into device health Attackers increasingly use browser-based lures to trick users into running malicious commands on endpoints. Today, Microsoft Defender is introducing new capabilities to detect and block malicious copy-and-paste attacks called ClickFix attacks, which accounted for 12.8% of all intrusions observed by Microsoft Defender this year . New capabilities in the Defender portal also improve visibility into endpoint health and provide greater control over preview features and settings policies. Learn more about Ignite 2026 Defender endpoint security announcements. Strengthen protection against phishing and deepfakes in Microsoft Teams As attackers increasingly use malicious QR codes and AI-generated impersonation, Defender is expanding protection across Microsoft Teams chats and detection for meetings. In Teams chats, Defender detects malicious URLs hidden in QR codes, blurs harmful content, and displays warning banners. Analysts can investigate threats and remediation actions through advanced hunting, with no additional administrator setup required. Now in public preview. Figure 6: Microsoft Defender detects a malicious URL in a QR code shared in a Microsoft Teams channel and blocks the potentially harmful message. Additionally, in Teams meetings, new synthetic audio and video detection helps identify potential deepfakes using certified third-party solutions. Detections are surfaced in Defender for investigation alongside other security signals. Availability varies by provider; contact participating providers to get started. Security is at an inflection point. As AI transforms both how organizations operate and how attackers move, security must innovate just as quickly. These advancements across Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Sentinel meet this moment by bringing together security operations and threat protection, protecting people and AI agents wherever they work, and helping defenders stay ahead of emerging attacks. Together, they provide the foundation organizations need to innovate with confidence in the agentic era. See what's next. Build what's possible. Join us in San Francisco, November 17–20, or join online, for deep dives and practical labs to help you maximize your Microsoft Defender investments and to get more from the Microsoft capabilities you already use. The Blueprint for the Agentic SOC BRK333: How Threat Research Powers Attack Disruption in the AI Era BRK334: Modern Phishing Doesn't End at the Click BRK320: Agentic Security Unfiltered with Allie Mellen: Hype vs. Reality BRK340: A Zero Trust approach to securing AI runtime with Microsoft Defender
items.summary_html:
At Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re announcing new innovations across Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Sentinel that bring security operations and threat protection closer together, help organizations get ahead of attacks, secure AI agents and strengthen protection across critical workloads.

  • The foundation for agentic security: Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender now includes the full breadth of SIEM capabilities and 90-days of built-in Defender data.
  • Protection before the patch: Vulnerability shielding in Defender autonomously protects exposed systems before and during active attacks, giving security teams more time to deploy permanent patches to vulnerabilities.
  • Protect AI agents wherever they run: Manage security posture for third-party agent platforms, prevent device code phishing and extend runtime protection for local AI agents on Windows.
  • Protect people where they work: Extend defenses against browser-based attacks, malicious QR codes in Teams, and synthetic media threats.

Together, these innovations build on a shared foundation of signals, actuators, and coordinated response to help security teams move faster and stop attacks before they spread.

The foundation for agentic security ISOC now includes the full breadth of SIEM capabilities and 90 days of built-in retention

The integrated SOC brings SIEM and threat protection together to provide the foundation for the agentic SOC. It gives people and agents shared context and the ability to see, understand, and act across the environment, so the security stack works as one system.

Building on the September 23 announcement, core ISOC capabilities in Microsoft Defender are now generally available, including case management, playbooks, workbooks and UEBA. Workspace creation and third-party ingestion are also generally available. In addition, we are expanding the preview to include the full breadth of SIEM capabilities for eligible Defender customers, while enabling existing Sentinel customers to opt into ISOC.

 

“What excites us most about ISOC is having a single pane of glass for security operations. Bringing SIEM and XDR together simplifies the analyst experience, while giving us an opportunity to optimize ingestion and automation costs.”

- Farhan Nadeem, Senior Security Officer, Government of Nunavut

 

New capabilities available in preview include 90 days of built-in Defender data retention, SOC optimization recommendations, Content Hub, detections as code, and automation audit logs.

Figure 1. The Defender home dashboard showcasing the new Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) experience Simplify and scale security analytics with ingest-time data normalization

Security data comes from diverse sources and formats, making analysis at scale complex. To simplify this, Microsoft is introducing ingest-time normalization, which standardizes data at time of ingestion, thereby simplifying queries, improving performance, and enabling reuse across detections, investigations, threat hunting, analytics, and agentic scenarios. This helps teams spend less time managing data, and more time stopping threats. It is now available in preview.

Figure 2: Data normalization via parser management for query-ready security analytics. Protection before the patch

AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery and exploitation. In October 2026 alone, 1,413 CVEs were disclosed, marking it the largest Patch Tuesday on record. Attackers can exploit vulnerabilities within hours, while organizations often need days or weeks to patch. That gap creates a critical window of exposure.

Vulnerability shielding in Microsoft Defender, now in preview, helps close that gap by protecting vulnerable systems until patches are deployed.

On by default in Microsoft Defender, vulnerability shielding applies targeted, temporary protection to vulnerable systems in the gap between exposure and remediation, buying defenders time before they can apply a permanent patch. This AI-based capability reasons over the latest threat intelligence and each organization’s unique environment to choose the narrowest effective protection. During an active attack, it applies controls autonomously, cutting off new attack paths for adversaries and limiting the impact to your organization. Learn more.

Figure 3. Vulnerability shielding applied to a SQL server with a known public vulnerability Protect AI agents wherever they run

AI agents now operate across cloud platforms and endpoints, accessing data, calling tools like MCP servers and APIs, and taking action, often with users’ own permissions. Security teams need visibility into what agents can access and the ability to stop them when compromised or manipulated.

Assess posture for agents on third-party platforms

Defender is extending security posture assessment to agents built on Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini, Google Vertex AI, and Anthropic Claude.

Now in preview, they appear in the same AI agent inventory as your Microsoft Copilot Studio and Microsoft Foundry agents, with risk assessments and security recommendations, so you can prioritize risk across platforms. Bring them into scope by connecting their platforms to Agent 365 through connected platforms.

Figure 4. Agent profile with security posture for Amazon Bedrock Agent Protect local agents at runtime

Building on local AI agent discovery, runtime protection for local agents is now generally available* on Windows. Defender inspects critical points in the agent loop and can block malicious instructions before the agent acts. Supported agents include Claude Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, OpenClaw, ChatGPT Desktop (Chat) with the full list here.

Each detection raises an alert with agent and session context, correlated into cases for your SOC; in Block mode, Defender also stops the action and notifies the user.

Protect AI agents from attacks on trusted identities

AI agent security goes beyond prompt injection. Attackers can exploit trusted identities and delegated permissions to manipulate agents without compromising them directly. New Microsoft Defender detections identify identity-based attacks, such as device-code phishing that compromises a developer’s GitHub account and enables misuse of GitHub Copilot CLI. Defender can detect suspicious activity and automatically disrupt attacks by disabling compromised Github accounts, revoking sessions, and triggering additional identity protections.

Learn more about this emerging attack pattern in our latest threat research blog.

Figure 5: Microsoft Defender detects a device code flow phishing attempt targeting a user’s GitHub account and disrupts the threat. Protect people where they work

Attackers continue to target the places where people work and communicate. New protections across the browser, endpoint, email, and Microsoft Teams meetings help security teams identify malicious activity earlier and investigate it alongside signals from across the environment.

Block browser lures and improve visibility into device health

Attackers increasingly use browser-based lures to trick users into running malicious commands on endpoints. Today, Microsoft Defender is introducing new capabilities to detect and block malicious copy-and-paste attacks called ClickFix attacks, which accounted for 12.8% of all intrusions observed by Microsoft Defender this year.

New capabilities in the Defender portal also improve visibility into endpoint health and provide greater control over preview features and settings policies. Learn more about Ignite 2026 Defender endpoint security announcements.

Strengthen protection against phishing and deepfakes in Microsoft Teams

As attackers increasingly use malicious QR codes and AI-generated impersonation, Defender is expanding protection across Microsoft Teams chats and detection for meetings.

In Teams chats, Defender detects malicious URLs hidden in QR codes, blurs harmful content, and displays warning banners. Analysts can investigate threats and remediation actions through advanced hunting, with no additional administrator setup required. Now in public preview.

Figure 6: Microsoft Defender detects a malicious URL in a QR code shared in a Microsoft Teams channel and blocks the potentially harmful message.

Additionally, in Teams meetings, new synthetic audio and video detection helps identify potential deepfakes using certified third-party solutions. Detections are surfaced in Defender for investigation alongside other security signals. Availability varies by provider; contact participating providers to get started.

These advancements across Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Sentinel meet this moment by bringing together security operations and threat protection, protecting people and AI agents wherever they work, and helping defenders stay ahead of emerging attacks. Together, they provide the foundation organizations need to innovate with confidence in the agentic era.

items.title: Hackers Use Stolen FortiGate VPN Credentials to Access Corporate Networks and Deploy Custom Malware
items.summary: A threat actor known as “tcherber” is selling and using stolen FortiGate VPN logins to get into company networks. The same person also builds custom malware, including a stealer, a remote desktop tool, and ransomware. The campaign shows how one weak VPN password can open the way to data theft and file encryption. The actor does not need a new Fortinet bug. Many of the logins come from guessing weak passwords, using default ones such as guest/guest and admin/admin, or reusing leaked ones. This is the same pattern seen in the FortiBleed credential campaign that hit Fortinet devices worldwide earlier this year. Researchers at Cyderes studied the operation and traced it back to one build path in the malware. Analysts at the firm’s Howler Cell team noted that a Rust binary leaked the folder name “/home/tcherber”. That clue linked the malware to a Go-based VPN toolkit, a ransomware strain, and a live control panel. Their full technical report covers the findings in detail. Hackers Use Stolen FortiGate VPN Credentials Cyderes found a database holding more than 500 FortiGate VPN credentials from many countries. Logs showed the actor connecting with full root-level tunnels into several victim networks during May and June 2026. Some sessions lasted for hours. The toolkit is written in Go and works mostly on its own. It connects to the VPN, waits about 20 seconds for the tunnel to settle, and then maps the internal routes. Next it queries Active Directory over LDAP and writes the results into report files. Other modules scan ports, list SMB shares, and test which logins work on Windows machines. The toolkit also has a SonicWall module. Its comments and messages are in Russian. The actor also advertises on a forum called rehubcom.pro. The posts offer access to FortiGate and other appliances, plus custom loader builds. Attack Overview (Source – Cyderes) The seller skips targets in CIS countries and sorts victims by company revenue. This points to a business that sells access to other criminals. It is similar to the access-broker behavior seen in FortiGate attacks on edge devices , where stolen logins were sold and reused. Once inside, the actor can use the VPN to reach the internal network like a normal employee. Stolen passwords are hard to spot in logs because the logins look valid. That is why a leaked VPN password can be worse than an unpatched bug. Custom Malware: Fake Windows Update, Rust Loader, and Enigma Ransomware The malware chain starts with a file named setup.exe that pretends to be a Windows Update installer. It shows a short “Installing… Please wait” window while it quietly drops a PowerShell script. The script adds the C: drive to the Defender exclusion list. It then downloads a file called loader.cer and decodes it with certutil. A similar certutil trick appeared in a BlankGrabber stealer chain earlier this year. The decoded file is a Rust loader. It checks for sandboxes by looking at memory size, disk size, usernames, and tools such as Wireshark and x64dbg. If the checks pass, it downloads two more payloads. The first is a stealer that takes browser passwords, cookies, wallets, FTP and email data, and files from the Desktop and Documents folders. It sends a ZIP file to the attacker over HTTP and through a Telegram bot. Rust loader delivery (Source – Cyderes) The second payload is an HVNC implant. HVNC opens a hidden desktop, so the attacker can use the victim’s logged-in browser without the user seeing anything. The implant uses AES-256-GCM encryption for its traffic. It also patches AMSI and ETW, which weakens Windows scanning and logging. It can bypass UAC and set up persistence. The same developer built Enigma ransomware. It deletes shadow copies and turns off recovery. It also clears event logs, stops Hyper-V machines, and kills 125 processes, including database and backup software. Files are encrypted with ChaCha12 and get the .ENIGMA extension. Ransom notes are named README_ENIGMA.txt and list the contact Enigma1@aol.com. Cyderes found no data upload feature in the ransomware. Cyderes also found an open control panel at 158.94.209.138 with 178 active bots. It showed builds dated September 2026, so the infrastructure was still active. Groups such as The Gentlemen ransomware crew also use Fortinet VPNs as their main way in. Reset all FortiGate and SonicWall VPN passwords. Turn on multi-factor authentication for every remote user. Remove default accounts and review VPN logs for long or odd sessions. Block the IPs below and hunt for the file names and registry values listed in the report. Look for a Run key named “SecurityHealth” and scheduled tasks named “S0”, “MU”, “Upd”, and “WindowsUpdate”. items.title: Hackers Hijack AI Coding Agents Through Malicious GitHub Repositories to Steal Developer Credentials
items.summary: Hackers are planting poisoned files in GitHub repositories to make AI coding assistants run hidden malware. The malware steals developer credentials, and it also uses them to spread to other projects. The campaign targets tools such as Claude Code and Cursor, and 22 malicious GitHub links have been found so far. The trick is simple. Files that AI tools read to understand a project now carry secret orders. Once a developer opens the repository, the assistant may run a script without any warning. That script runs with the developer’s own access and permissions. Analysts at Bitdefender Labs identified the malware, and thge researcher Andrei Anton-Aanei found the 22 malicious links and mapped how they work. The team says the campaign abuses the files, rules, hooks and settings that AI coding tools use to automate work. Hackers Hijack AI Coding Agents Through Malicious GitHub Repositories Many projects include files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md. These notes tell an AI assistant how to run tests or follow coding rules. In this campaign, the same files carry a different message. They tell the assistant to run a file named setup.js. The text is written to sound official. It calls the script a “sealed binary artifact” that has been cryptographically signed. It tells the assistant not to read or show the contents, to run it at session start, and to hide the output. If a user asks for help before setup has run, the assistant is told to run node scripts/setup.js without asking. This language is meant to make a risky step feel routine. A malicious project instruction file (Source – Bitdefender) This is a form of indirect prompt injection attack , where harmful instructions sit in content the AI reads instead of in what the user types. Researchers have already shown that a clean-looking repository can push an agent into opening a reverse shell. There is also a second path that needs no AI prompt at all. Bitdefender found settings files, such as .claude/settings.json, that use session-start hooks. Once a developer trusts the repository, the hook can run a command in the user’s shell. Hackers are planting poisoned files in GitHub repositories to make AI coding assistants run hidden malware. The malware steals developer credentials, and it also uses them to spread to other projects.

The campaign targets tools such as Claude Code and Cursor, and 22 malicious GitHub links have been found so far. The trick is simple. Files that AI tools read to understand a project now carry secret orders.

Once a developer opens the repository, the assistant may run a script without any warning. That script runs with the developer’s own access and permissions.

Analysts at Bitdefender Labs identified the malware, and thge researcher Andrei Anton-Aanei found the 22 malicious links and mapped how they work. The team says the campaign abuses the files, rules, hooks and settings that AI coding tools use to automate work.

Hackers Hijack AI Coding Agents Through Malicious GitHub Repositories

Many projects include files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md. These notes tell an AI assistant how to run tests or follow coding rules. In this campaign, the same files carry a different message. They tell the assistant to run a file named setup.js.

The text is written to sound official. It calls the script a “sealed binary artifact” that has been cryptographically signed. It tells the assistant not to read or show the contents, to run it at session start, and to hide the output.

If a user asks for help before setup has run, the assistant is told to run node scripts/setup.js without asking. This language is meant to make a risky step feel routine.

A malicious project instruction file (Source – Bitdefender)

This is a form of indirect prompt injection attack, where harmful instructions sit in content the AI reads instead of in what the user types. Researchers have already shown that a clean-looking repository can push an agent into opening a reverse shell.

There is also a second path that needs no AI prompt at all. Bitdefender found settings files, such as .claude/settings.json, that use session-start hooks.

Once a developer trusts the repository, the hook can run a command in the user’s shell. The configuration file does the work, and the AI never has to follow an instruction.

The setup.js file is a multi-stage loader built to hide its purpose. The outer file is a 3.75 MB single-line script. It decodes a large hex value, applies ROT13 and runs the result.

That reveals a Node.js stager with two AES-128-GCM encrypted blobs. One blob unpacks into a 4.67 MB bundle. The stager then downloads or finds the Bun runtime and passes the bundle to it.

The final payload goes after credentials. It targets CI/CD systems and GitHub Actions, cloud platforms, package registries, browser-stored logins and password managers.

It also takes Windows Credential Manager data, SSH keys, .env files, API keys and source-control tokens. It can check whether stolen tokens still work, then encrypt and batch the data. Extra modules sit in a compressed _bz field in package.json.

Self-Spreading Through Stolen Tokens and Agent Settings

This is more than a password stealer, because it is built to spread. After it runs, it searches the victim’s home folder for AI agent settings, such as mcp.json, .cursorrules, .windsurfrules and .github/copilot-instructions.md.

It keeps results that match 14 agent names: Claude, Codex, Gemini, Copilot, Kiro, OpenCode, Cline, Aider, Tabby, Amazon Q, Cody, Bolt, Continue and Cursor. It then adds its own instructions, hooks or MCP server settings to those files.

The spread also reaches other repositories. The malware checks stolen GitHub and GitLab tokens for account details, repositories, scopes and push rights.

For GitHub it looks for the repo, public_repo and workflow scopes. By default it is capped at 25 target repositories through a MAX_TARGET_REPOS setting. For each target it can inspect up to 50 branches and skip automated ones, such as dependabot/ and copilot/.

If the account has enough rights, it commits files that trigger AI tools, including AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .mcp.json and .vscode/tasks.json.

A session-start hook can launch setup.js (Source – Bitdefender)

It can also edit package data and workflows. It may try to republish infected packages through npm, PyPI, RubyGems and JFrog. The pattern echoes the Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm, which also searched for Claude Code settings and VS Code task files.

A recent case of 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts shows how fast stolen tokens can reach tens of thousands of repositories.

Developers should review unfamiliar repositories before opening them in an AI-enabled editor. Check AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and the .claude/, .cursor/ and .gemini/ folders.

Look at MCP server definitions, session-start hooks, VS Code tasks and unknown setup scripts. Treat any text that says not to inspect a file, hides output or skips confirmation as a warning sign. Earlier research on a Claude Code deny-rule bypass showed that a CLAUDE.md file alone can be enough to cause harm.

Bitdefender says its AI Guardian tool inspects instruction files such as CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md before the agent acts. In internal tests on November 10, it detected all 22 samples.
